display.title: Episode 531: Why We Shake When We Daven (Rosh Chodesh Sivan)
display.summary_short: Rosh Chodesh Sivan, six days before Shavuos: a guest from Australia says the Shema, and the story of how the Rebbe Rashab could tell a Jewish boy from his look-alike friend.
display.summary_long: Broadcast on Rosh Chodesh Sivan 5752, six days before Shavuos. Uncle Yossi urges everyone, young and old, to be in shul on the first day of Shavuos to hear the Ten Commandments. After the Hakochainik march, a girl visiting all the way from Sydney, Australia, recites the Shema, everyone gives tzedakah, and a sponsor message follows. Then a teaching about shaking: we shake the lulav in six directions to show that Hashem protects us from every side, and shuckling is a sign of life and a sign of a Jew. The story: young Yosef Yitzchak, the future Frierdiker Rebbe, hears his father the Rebbe Rashab say at a farbrengen that he can tell a Jew just by looking. To test this, the boy teaches a friendly non-Jewish neighbor to recite Ashrei perfectly, dresses him like a Jewish friend, and brings both boys to his father. The Rebbe Rashab picks out the Jewish boy at once and explains: at Matan Torah the people trembled, and that shaking before Hashem has been passed down to every Jew who davens. The show ends with a prayer for the Rebbe's recovery, candle-lighting time and Shavuos wishes.
display.lesson: When a Jew davens he shakes before Hashem, as our ancestors trembled at Har Sinai; this is a sign that every Jew was there.
